title: The Scope Creep Crisis
setup: You run a six-person team and your Data Migration project is 75 percent done. In today's standup the PM quietly added three new requirements and reminded everyone the launch date has not moved. Your two seniors are already at capacity, and the last late project cost you a good engineer. Whatever you choose, the PM reports it up to the VP on Friday.
question: How do you handle the scope creep while protecting your team?

decisions.reasoning: Push back diplomatically with data showing impact
decisions.feedback: Scope negotiation protects your team from churn. Short-term stakeholder friction is worth long-term delivery reliability. This is the sustainable choice.
decisions.tradeoffs: Stakeholders may be disappointed initially, but they'll respect your discipline when you deliver on time.
decisions.profileNote: This cautious approach prevents technical debt and protects team health.

decisions.reasoning: Add senior talent to absorb the extra scope
decisions.synergy: A Tech Lead sets direction while pair programming spreads that context to the rest of the team, so the added scope does not rest on one person.
decisions.feedback: Throwing people at scope creep is expensive. Works short-term but creates technical debt and risks burnout. The Tech Lead helps but can't prevent all churn.
decisions.tradeoffs: You meet the deadline but your team pays the price. Watch for turnover next quarter.
decisions.profileNote: Delegators often over-staff to absorb pressure. Consider if scope is truly valuable.

decisions.reasoning: You personally take on the extra scope
decisions.feedback: Hero mode delivers short-term but creates learned helplessness. Your team doesn't grow when you do all the hard work. You're also taking on massive technical debt alone.
decisions.tradeoffs: Stakeholders love the save, but your team resents being sidelined. Combined with burnout risk.
decisions.profileNote: Classic hero profile. Delivers at massive personal and team cost.

decisions.reasoning: Bring in external help to handle overflow
decisions.feedback: Contractors provide flexible capacity but require onboarding and create knowledge silos. A reasonable middle ground that buys time.
decisions.tradeoffs: Extra cost but spreads workload. Watch for contractor dependencies and documentation gaps.
decisions.profileNote: Delegated solution. Works if contractors are plug-and-play.

title: The Hero Burnout
setup: Your strongest engineer has quietly become the team's single point of failure. They ship every hard fix, review every PR at midnight, and field every Slack ping, while the other four have stopped stepping up. Their last one-on-one ended with 'I'm fine, it's just this quarter.' You have maybe two quarters before they burn out and walk, taking the only working knowledge of the billing system with them.
question: How do you de-escalate the hero and rebuild the team?

decisions.reasoning: Force knowledge sharing and pair the hero with others
decisions.synergy: Knowledge Transfer moves what the hero knows out of their head, and Pair Programming makes the rest of the team practice using it.
decisions.feedback: Perfect counter to hero mode! Knowledge transfer breaks the silo, pair programming forces collaboration. Short-term slowdown for long-term team health. Your hero might resist but it's leadership's job to protect them from themselves.
decisions.tradeoffs: Hero won't like this. Be ready for tough conversations about sustainable pace.
decisions.profileNote: Delegator counters hero by forcing distribution. This is the play.

decisions.reasoning: Capture knowledge before it's lost
decisions.synergy: Documentation captures the system on paper and Code Review keeps more eyes on changes, so knowledge stops living in one person.
decisions.feedback: Documentation provides insurance but doesn't solve the root problem. Code review spreads knowledge slowly. Better than nothing but slower than forced pairing.
decisions.tradeoffs: Safer politically but less immediate impact on hero behavior.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious approach. Works but takes longer.

decisions.reasoning: Let the hero continue - they're delivering
decisions.feedback: Disaster in waiting. You're getting short-term delivery but team morale is collapsing and tech debt is compounding. When (not if) your hero quits, you'll have a catastrophe.
decisions.tradeoffs: Stakeholders happy now, catastrophic failure looming.
decisions.profileNote: Playing into hero mode. Worst long-term outcome.

title: The Platform Strategy Bet
setup: The CEO pulled you aside after the board dinner: turn the internal tooling into a product and it could be a 50 million dollar line. It would take twelve engineers for a year, pulled straight off the core roadmap, into a market where two competitors already have logos and signed contracts. The board wants a recommendation, not a maybe. If the bet is wrong, it is your name on the deck.
question: Do you bet the company on platform strategy?

decisions.reasoning: Validate demand before full commitment
decisions.synergy: Market Analysis tells you whether demand is real and the MVP proves it with the smallest possible build, so you commit only after both agree.
decisions.feedback: Perfect innovation profile play! Validate before committing. Market analysis de-risks the bet. MVP proves demand with minimal investment. You keep optionality while exploring upside.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slower path to revenue but much higher probability of success. Board might push for bigger bet.
decisions.profileNote: Innovator profile: high conviction but disciplined validation.

decisions.reasoning: Full commitment - go big or go home
decisions.feedback: High-risk, high-reward. If platform succeeds, you're a hero. If it fails (70% chance for new platforms), you've derailed core product and burned team morale. Classic hero profile - personal bet on big outcome.
decisions.tradeoffs: Career-defining decision. Make sure you have board/air cover if it fails.
decisions.profileNote: Hero move. Huge upside but massive risk concentration.

decisions.reasoning: De-risk through partnership or acquisition
decisions.synergy: Build vs Buy sizes the true cost of building alone and a Partnership shares that cost and risk with someone who already has the market.
decisions.feedback: Smart risk mitigation. Partnership shares investment and validates demand. Acquisition shortcuts build vs buy. More expensive but faster and lower risk than organic build.
decisions.tradeoffs: Lower margin but higher probability. Good delegation strategy.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: navigator, finds low-risk paths.

title: The CI/CD Pipeline Crisis
setup: Two out of every five deploys fail, and your team now budgets an hour of pipeline roulette into every release. Engineers paste the same red build logs into the channel daily and morale is visibly sagging. Leadership has heard the complaints but still expects this quarter's features on time. Every week you defer the real fix, the flakiness spreads to more services.
question: How do you tackle the pipeline crisis without halting development?

decisions.reasoning: Incremental improvements while keeping pipeline running
decisions.synergy: CI/CD Improvements clear the worst pipeline pain while Automated Testing keeps regressions from creeping back in as you go.
decisions.feedback: Prudent approach. You fix the worst issues first while keeping features flowing. Teams see immediate relief on common pain points. Takes discipline to not just rewrite everything.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slower total fix but zero downtime. Stakeholders see progress every week.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: minimize risk, incremental gains compound.

decisions.reasoning: You personally dive in and fix everything in one marathon session
decisions.synergy: A marathon Debug Session plus Heroic Programming lets one person force a fix fast, at the cost of the team ever owning it.
decisions.feedback: Classic hero move. You save the day but create dependency. Team learns that crises get 'hero'd' so they don't step up. You're also exhausted and behind on your actual work.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast fix, slow death of team ownership. You'll be debugging alone forever.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile delivers but destroys team resilience.

decisions.reasoning: Replace the whole pipeline with modern tools
decisions.feedback: Big bet that pays off if successful. You're down for a quarter but emerge with state-of-the-art tooling. High risk - migrations fail 30% of the time and you'd be in worse shape.
decisions.tradeoffs: All-or-nothing. If it works you're a legend. If it fails you're rebuilding from zero.
decisions.profileNote: Innovator profile: big bets for big gains. Timing is everything.

decisions.reasoning: Lock in behavior with tests before touching pipeline
decisions.synergy: Documentation forces you to understand the current pipeline and Testing locks that behavior in before you change anything.
decisions.feedback: Smart! Testing gives you safety net. Documentation forces you to understand current state. Slower start but much safer changes. Tests catch regressions during fixes.
decisions.tradeoffs: Upfront investment pays dividends. You can't fix what you don't understand.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: measure twice, cut once.

title: The Performance Bottleneck
setup: Payment latency jumped from 200 milliseconds to two seconds at peak and checkout is timing out. Finance says every hour of this costs about 50 thousand dollars in dropped orders, and the CEO is now in your DMs asking for an update every fifteen minutes. The cause is not obvious: it could be the database, the network, or a third-party API you do not control. Your team is staring at you, waiting for a call.
question: How do you approach the performance crisis?

decisions.reasoning: Systematic profiling with proper measurement
decisions.synergy: Automated Testing measures where the time actually goes so Performance Optimization targets the real bottleneck instead of a guess.
decisions.feedback: Methodical approach. You instrument everything, find the actual bottleneck (not the guess), and fix it properly. Takes 3 hours of measurement but saves 3 days of wrong fixes.
decisions.tradeoffs: Delay is painful but fixing the right thing is faster than fixing everything.
decisions.profileNote: Innovator profile: use tools and data, not intuition.

decisions.reasoning: Intense debugging session - you trust your gut
decisions.synergy: A Debug Session driven by Heroic Programming bets on one person's intuition to find the cause quickly, with high variance either way.
decisions.feedback: You're rolling dice with production. Maybe you get lucky and guess right. Maybe you waste 4 hours down wrong path while transactions keep dropping. Even if you win, you taught team that heroics beat process.
decisions.tradeoffs: High variance. Right guess = fast fix. Wrong guess = catastrophic delay.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile: high risk, high reward, unsustainable.

decisions.reasoning: Review architecture before touching code
decisions.synergy: Technical Due Diligence surfaces the systemic issues and Architecture Review decides how to fix the foundation rather than the symptom.
decisions.feedback: Slowest start, strongest finish. You discover the architecture has systemic issues that quick fixes won't solve. You fix the foundation instead of patching symptoms. Quarter-long solution but permanent.
decisions.tradeoffs: CEO will be mad for a week, then impressed for a year.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: fix the system, not the symptom.

decisions.reasoning: Apply known performance patterns quickly
decisions.feedback: You apply low-hanging fruit: add indexes, increase cache, optimize queries. Gets you from 2s to 400ms in 2 hours. Not perfect but buys breathing room for proper fix. Strategic compromise.
decisions.tradeoffs: Good enough for now. True fix still needed later.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: manage expectations while delivering value.

title: The Security Vulnerability
setup: An auditor just flagged a critical vulnerability in production and a working exploit is already public on GitHub. Patching cleanly means downtime during your busiest hours, a workaround is faster but leaves gaps, and a full review is safest but slow. Legal and your VP both want a plan within the hour. Every hour it stays open, the odds of a real breach climb.
question: How do you handle the security crisis?

decisions.reasoning: Patch immediately with full testing
decisions.synergy: Patching the Security Vulnerability closes the hole and Automated Testing proves the fix holds before it ships under pressure.
decisions.feedback: Perfect security response. You accept short-term pain (downtime) for long-term safety. Testing ensures fix works. Stakeholders trust your decisiveness. Security is non-negotiable.
decisions.tradeoffs: Downtime costs revenue but breach costs everything.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: do it right, do it once.

decisions.reasoning: Quick workaround to stop immediate threat
decisions.feedback: Temporary patches create technical debt. You stop the bleeding but the wound needs proper surgery. Risk: workaround might have holes. You also have to remember to do the real fix later.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast now, pay later. Hope you remember to come back.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: manage perception, defer real work.

decisions.reasoning: You personally code the fix over 20 hours
decisions.synergy: Heroic Programming lets you code the Security Vulnerability fix alone and fast, but leaves the team unable to respond next time.
decisions.feedback: You save the day but create dependency. Team doesn't learn how to respond to security issues. You burn out. Next crisis, everyone waits for the hero instead of acting. Also you're single point of failure.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast fix, slow team death. Unsustainable security model.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile: personal sacrifice for company safety.

decisions.reasoning: Pair senior devs to fix together
decisions.synergy: Pair Programming puts two seniors on the fix together and Code Review spreads the security patterns, building capability while closing the hole.
decisions.feedback: Best long-term play. Two seniors collaborate, both learn security response patterns, knowledge spreads. Slower initially but builds organizational capability. Next security issue, team handles without you.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slower start but sustainable security culture.
decisions.profileNote: Delegator profile: build team capability, not hero stories.

title: The Team Burnout Crisis
setup: Velocity is down 40 percent and your one-on-ones all tell the same story: too many urgent projects, constant context switching, and weekend work that has quietly become the norm. Three people have freshened up their LinkedIn and one has a dentist appointment every Thursday afternoon. Leadership does not see a burnout problem, they see a delivery problem, and they want the team back on track. You have one quarter before the resignations start landing.
question: How do you address the burnout crisis?

decisions.reasoning: Listen to team first before making changes
decisions.synergy: 1:1 Meetings surface what people will only say privately and the Team Meeting turns those signals into a shared diagnosis.
decisions.feedback: You discover the real issues: two people are carrying the team, everyone else is in meetings, and priorities change daily. Team feels heard immediately. Morale improves before you even fix anything. Now you know what to fix.
decisions.tradeoffs: Takes time but gives you correct diagnosis. Better than guessing.
decisions.profileNote: Delegator profile: listen first, then lead.

decisions.reasoning: Negotiate relief from leadership
decisions.synergy: Risk Assessment gives you the evidence and Scope Negotiation uses it to buy the team real relief from leadership.
decisions.feedback: You push back hard on leadership: 'team will deliver 30% less for 1 quarter to recover.' Stakeholders are mad initially, but see improved quality next quarter. Team feels protected and rallies. Trust in your leadership solidifies.
decisions.tradeoffs: Political capital spent, but earns team loyalty. Long-term win.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: manage up to protect down.

decisions.reasoning: Document and standardize to reduce chaos
decisions.synergy: Documentation removes the daily cognitive load and Risk Assessment catches failures before they become fires, cutting chaos at both ends.
decisions.feedback: You create runbooks for common tasks, document architecture, and add risk reviews to planning. Removes cognitive load. Team stops reinventing wheels. Burnout drops 30% just from reduced chaos.
decisions.tradeoffs: Boring but effective. Process reduces friction.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: systematic fixes for systematic problems.

decisions.reasoning: Push team harder to hit targets
decisions.feedback: Disaster. You get short-term velocity boost but accelerate departures. Two more people quit. Team stops trusting you. You're now known as the manager who chose targets over people. Recovery takes quarters.
decisions.tradeoffs: Career suicide. Never worth it.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile applied to management - maximum damage.

title: The Promotion Dilemma
setup: The promotion cycle closes in two weeks and you have two slots for five engineers who all earned it. Leadership wants objective decisions but has already hinted at two favorites who are not your strongest people. Whoever you pass over will hear about it, and the team is watching to see whether effort actually gets rewarded here. Get this wrong and it reads as favoritism for the rest of the year.
question: How do you decide who gets promoted?

decisions.reasoning: Create objective promotion framework with clear criteria
decisions.synergy: Documentation writes down the criteria and a Data-Driven Pitch backs each candidate with evidence, so the decision reads as fair rather than personal.
decisions.feedback: Brilliant! You create scorecard: impact, technical depth, mentorship, values. Share with team and leadership. Everyone knows the rules. Decisions feel fair even to people who didn't get promoted. Creates culture of meritocracy.
decisions.tradeoffs: Takes time to create framework but pays dividends forever.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: align stakeholders on process, not just outcomes.

decisions.reasoning: Be transparent about constraints and let team help decide
decisions.synergy: Transparency puts the real constraints on the table and 1:1 Meetings let each person respond, making the process feel collaborative.
decisions.feedback: You share the brutal truth: '2 slots, 5 people, all deserving. Let's discuss criteria together.' Team appreciates honesty. People self-nominate with evidence. Process feels collaborative not competitive. Those passed over respect the process.
decisions.tradeoffs: Vulnerable but builds trust. Transparency beats perfect decisions.
decisions.profileNote: Transparency is its own strategy.

decisions.reasoning: Align leadership on criteria then decide
decisions.synergy: A Data-Driven Pitch arms the Executive Review with evidence, so leadership aligns on criteria instead of defaulting to favorites.
decisions.feedback: You spend time with executives: 'Here are the 5 candidates, here are their strengths, who are we optimizing for?' Get alignment on criteria. Remind them favorites don't always equal best. Push for fairness. Takes political capital.
decisions.tradeoffs: Protects team from executive whim but requires relationship capital.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: manage up to protect down.

decisions.reasoning: Use your judgment, announce decisions
decisions.feedback: Worst approach. Even if your picks are 'right', process feels arbitrary. People who didn't get promoted resent you. Team thinks it's favoritism. You lose trust. Morale drops and your top performers start looking elsewhere.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast decision, long-term damage.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile: manager knows best. Never works.

title: The Skip-Level Surprise
setup: Your VP opened your one-on-one by reading back anonymous feedback from your own team: people feel disconnected from strategy, the work feels reactive, and Project X is seen as busywork. You had no idea any of this was brewing, and the VP wants a plan by Monday. Your team does not know this conversation happened. How you respond decides whether your VP still trusts your read on your own group.
question: How do you respond to the executive feedback?

decisions.reasoning: Acknowledge gap, get data, present plan
decisions.synergy: The Team Meeting gathers the real picture from your group and the Executive Review turns it into a plan you can own in front of the VP.
decisions.feedback: Perfect play. You tell VP: 'You're right, I missed this, here's my data gathering plan, I'll present findings Friday.' Show humility + action. Team sees you take feedback seriously. You turn crisis into trust-building.
decisions.tradeoffs: Short-term credibility hit for long-term leadership growth.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: turn feedback into action, not defensiveness.

decisions.reasoning: Defend with data that team is wrong
decisions.feedback: Disaster. You argue team is wrong, VP thinks you're out of touch. Team hears you're dismissing their concerns. You lose trust both directions. Creates perception you can't handle feedback.
decisions.tradeoffs: Defensive wins argument, loses war.
decisions.profileNote: Hero profile: defend self instead of listening.

decisions.reasoning: Make feedback process transparent
decisions.synergy: Transparency shares the feedback openly and Stakeholder Alignment turns it into a solution built with the people it affects.
decisions.feedback: You share VP feedback with team: 'Here's what I heard, let's discuss.' Team appreciates transparency. You co-create solution. VP sees you including team. Turns feedback into collaborative problem-solving.
decisions.tradeoffs: Vulnerable but builds trust at all levels.
decisions.profileNote: Transparency creates alignment naturally.

decisions.reasoning: Quick team session then present fixes
decisions.synergy: Transparency names the feedback honestly and a fast Team Meeting converts it into concrete changes within the week.
decisions.feedback: You move fast: team session Monday, VP presentation Friday with 3 concrete changes. Shows you take it seriously. Some fixes are wrong (you moved too fast) but course-correct as you learn.
decisions.tradeoffs: Fast action with some mistakes beats perfect planning with no action.
decisions.profileNote: Delegator profile: rapid iteration with team input.

title: The M&A Negotiation
setup: Your company just closed a 50 million dollar acquisition of a 30-person startup, and now you own the integration. Their CEO wants the VP Engineering title and full autonomy, their stack is incompatible with yours, and they ship to production with no tests and a move-fast culture. The board expects synergy numbers in two quarters. Push too hard and the talent you paid for walks; too soft and you have two companies under one roof with nothing to show.
question: How do you integrate the acquisition?

decisions.reasoning: Create bridge team with engineers from both sides
decisions.synergy: A Bridge Team learns both systems from the inside and Culture Integration grows shared norms from the bottom up rather than by decree.
decisions.feedback: Perfect M&A play. Two engineers from each side form integration team. They learn each other's systems, create translation layer, document differences. Preserves startup speed while adding enterprise reliability. Culture integration from bottom-up, not top-down.
decisions.tradeoffs: Slows them slightly but prevents culture clash catastrophe.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: align interests, preserve value.

decisions.reasoning: Re-architect their entire system in 1 quarter
decisions.synergy: A Tiger Team rebuilds on your platform while the Sunset Plan retires the old stack, forcing a clean cutover at high people risk.
decisions.feedback: High-risk technical play. You move their entire stack to your platform in 90 days. If successful, perfect integration. But 60% chance startup engineers quit (they didn't join to be enterprise). You might lose the talent you paid for.
decisions.tradeoffs: Technical perfection vs people retention. People usually win.
decisions.profileNote: Innovator profile: platform thinking, high technical risk.

decisions.reasoning: Leave them independent, document interfaces
decisions.synergy: Technical Due Diligence maps their system and Documentation pins down the interfaces, keeping the two sides stable but separate.
decisions.feedback: You keep them separate and document APIs. They stay fast, you stay stable. But synergy targets fail - you're just two companies under one roof. Board questions why you acquired them. No technical integration means no cost savings.
decisions.tradeoffs: Preserves culture but fails acquisition thesis. Board will be unhappy.
decisions.profileNote: Cautious profile: avoid conflict, but miss opportunity.

decisions.reasoning: Focus on culture integration before technical
decisions.synergy: Culture Integration builds the relationships first so the later Technical Due Diligence becomes collaborative instead of combative.
decisions.feedback: You spend Q1 on joint offsites, shared values, unified vision. Engineers build relationships. Q2 technical integration becomes collaborative not combative. Culture alignment unlocks technical alignment. Most important M&A success factor.
decisions.tradeoffs: Soft skills beat technical wizardry in M&A. Culture clash kills more deals than tech debt.
decisions.profileNote: Politician profile: people first, systems second.
